name: Gola Rainforest National Park
blurb: Upper Guinea rainforest where chimps, pygmy hippos and crowned eagles share the canopy.

tip.title: Fell the fig trees
tip.text: Figs feed elephants, monkeys, hornbills and chimpanzees. Set Fig trees to -100% and watch fruit-eaters drop, then the monkeys, chimps and eagles that depend on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Light reaching the canopy drives the forest; very little of it penetrates to the dim understorey.

nodes.name: Heavy rainfall
nodes.desc: The forest sits in a very wet part of West Africa, and the rains keep its streams, swamps and soils moist.

nodes.name: Forest soil and leaf litter
nodes.desc: Fallen leaves, fruit and wood rot into a thin nutrient layer that the trees and ferns draw on.

nodes.name: Streams and swamps
nodes.desc: Rivers and wet hollows give shy water-loving animals such as the pygmy hippo daytime cover and cool, moist ground.

nodes.name: Fungi and bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead leaves, wood, dung and carcasses in the warm, damp forest, returning nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Fig trees
nodes.desc: Figs fruit through much of the year in tropical forests, which makes them a dependable food for many monkeys, birds and mammals.

nodes.name: African oil palm
nodes.desc: A West African palm whose oily fruits are eaten by chimpanzees, elephants and rodents.

nodes.name: Plagiosiphon
nodes.desc: A rainforest tree or shrub of West Africa often found near rivers. Colobus monkeys are recorded eating it in GloBI.

nodes.name: Forkedfern
nodes.desc: A tangle-forming fern of forest clearings and openings, recorded in the Gola area. Ferns and herbs are staple foods of the pygmy hippo.

nodes.name: African forest elephant
nodes.desc: A forest-dwelling elephant that eats bark, leaves and many fruits, and spreads seeds over long distances. Its population in Gola has dwindled.

nodes.name: Pygmy hippopotamus
nodes.desc: A shy nocturnal hippo that hides in rivers by day and forages at dusk on herbs, ferns and fallen fruit. Gola is one of its refuges.

nodes.name: Western red colobus
nodes.desc: A leaf-eating monkey of the forest canopy, recorded eating Plagiosiphon. It is prey for chimpanzees and crowned eagles.

nodes.name: Olive colobus
nodes.desc: A small, secretive leaf-eating monkey of the lower forest levels, also recorded eating Plagiosiphon.

nodes.name: Diana monkey
nodes.desc: A canopy guenon that eats fruit and insects. It is hunted by chimpanzees, leopards and crowned eagles.

nodes.name: Yellow-casqued hornbill
nodes.desc: A large canopy hornbill, the most-recorded bird near Gola. It lives in family groups and is listed as Vulnerable.

nodes.name: Gambian pouched rat
nodes.desc: A large forest-edge rodent that eats fruit, nuts and other plant matter and is prey for many carnivores.

nodes.name: Royal antelope
nodes.desc: One of the smallest antelopes in the world, a shy browser of leaves, shoots and fallen fruit in dense forest.

nodes.name: Western chimpanzee
nodes.desc: An omnivore that eats fruit and hunts monkeys. Gola holds a population of over 300.

nodes.name: African harrier-hawk
nodes.desc: A raptor with flexible legs that probes cavities and nests for prey. It is often recorded near the park.

nodes.name: Pardine genet
nodes.desc: A small spotted nocturnal carnivore of West African forests that hunts rodents and other small animals.

nodes.name: African palm civet
nodes.desc: A tree-living nocturnal omnivore that eats fruit as well as small animals.

nodes.name: Leopard
nodes.desc: The top mammalian predator of the forest. It takes mid-sized prey such as monkeys and duikers, and smaller carnivores like genets.

nodes.name: Crowned eagle
nodes.desc: A powerful forest eagle that nests in tall trees and takes mostly monkeys, including colobus and Diana monkeys, and small antelopes.
